Kernels of linear maps

A generalization of Duistermaat and Van der Kallens theorem
Arno van den Essen Affiliation: Radboud University, Nijmegen    Jan Schoone Affiliation: Digital Security, Radboud University, Nijmegen E-mail: jan.schoone@ru.nl
Received: date / Accepted: date
Abstract

The theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen from 1998 proved the first case of the Mathieu conjecture. Using the theory of Mathieu-Zhao spaces, we can reformulate this theorem as Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is a Mathieu-Zhao space where LL is the linear map

L:𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn,X1,…,Xn−1]→𝐂,f↦f0.\displaystyle L\colon{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n},X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}^{-1}]\to{\bf C},\ f\mapsto f_{0}.

In this paper, we generalize this result (for n=1n=1) to all non-trivial linear maps L:𝐂⁡[X,X−1]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}]\to{\bf C} such that {Xn∣|n|≥N}⊂Ker⁡L\{X^{n}\mid|n|\geq N\}\subset\operatorname{Ker}L for some N≥1N\geq 1.

Keywords: 
algebraic geometry commutative algebra mathieu-zhao spaces mathieu conjecture

1 Introduction

In 1939, Ott-Heinrich Keller [4] formulated what is now known as the Jacobian conjecture:

Conjecture 1 (Jacobian conjecture)

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero and F∈k​[X1,…,Xn]nF\in k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]^{n} a polynomial mapping such that its Jacobian determinant JFJ_{F} is a non-zero constant. Then FF has an inverse function G∈k​[X1,…,Xn]nG\in k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]^{n}.

Since then, this conjecture remained unsolved (apart from the case n=1n=1). For a historical treaty and a collection of results around the Jacobian conjecture, one can read [2] and [3]. In 1997, Olivier Mathieu showed in [5] that the Jacobian conjecture follows from what is now known as the Mathieu conjecture:

Conjecture 2 (Mathieu conjecture)

Let GG be a compact connected real Lie group with Haar measure σ\sigma. Let ff be a complex valued GG-finite function on GG such that ∫Gfm​𝑑σ=0\int_{G}f^{m}d\sigma=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1. Then for every GG-finite function gg on GG, also ∫Gg​fm​𝑑σ=0\int_{G}gf^{m}d\sigma=0 for all large mm.

The Mathieu conjecture has been proved for the case of connected abelian groups by Duistermaat and Van der Kallen in 1998 [1].

From the formulation of the Mathieu conjecture, Wenhua Zhao formulated the notion of Mathieu-Zhao spaces that are a generalization of ideals. For history and details, see [12] and [3].

Together with this formulation, we manage to prove a generalization of the theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen in dimension one.

2 Notations and conventions

We write 𝐙{\bf Z} for the ring of integers, 𝐂{\bf C} for the field of complex numbers, and 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} for a finite field of qq elements. Furthermore, we always assume all rings to be commutative and to have an identity. Similarly, we assume all algebras to be unital and associative.

3 Mathieu-Zhao spaces and partial fractions decomposition

Because of the shape of the statement in the Mathieu conjecture [5], we can define the following generalisation of ideals in associative algebras, which we call Mathieu-Zhao spaces.

Definition 1

Let RR be any ring and AA an RR-algebra. For any subset MM of AA we define the radical of MM by

r(M):={a∈A∣∀m≫0:am∈M}\displaystyle r(M):=\{a\in A\mid\forall m\gg 0:a^{m}\in M\}

with m≫0m\gg 0 meaning all m≥Nm\geq N for some N≥1N\geq 1.

Remark 1

For an ideal II of RR, this coincides with the usual definition of the radical of II, being:

I:={a∈R∣∃n:an∈I}.\displaystyle\sqrt{I}:=\{a\in R\mid\exists n:a^{n}\in I\}.

It is well-known that the radical of an ideal is an ideal itself, and hence all an+ia^{n+i} are elements of II for i≥0i\geq 0.

Definition 2

Let RR be any ring and AA an RR-algebra. For any subset MM of AA we define the (left) strong radical of MM by

sr(M):={a∈A∣∀b∈A∀m≫0:bam∈M}.\displaystyle sr(M):=\{a\in A\mid\forall b\in A\ \forall m\gg 0:ba^{m}\in M\}.
Remark 2

Note that if a∈s​r​(M)a\in sr(M), then 1⋅am∈M1\cdot a^{m}\in M for all m≫0m\gg 0, hence a∈r⁡(M)a\in r(M). So we always have s​r​(M)⊂r⁡(M)sr(M)\subset r(M).

Definition 3

Let RR be any ring and AA an RR-algebra. We say that an RR-submodule MM of AA is a Mathieu-Zhao space of AA (short: MZ-space) if and only if s​r​(M)=r⁡(M)sr(M)=r(M).

A little less is needed in practice. Define r′(M)={a∈A∣∀m≥1:am∈M}r^{\prime}(M)=\{a\in A\mid\forall m\geq 1:a^{m}\in M\}. If r′​(M)⊂s​r​(M)r^{\prime}(M)\subset sr(M), then MM is an MZ-space of AA.

Proposition 1 ([3])

Let RR be a ring and AA an RR-algebra. Let MM be an additive subset of AA and I⊂AI\subset A an ideal of AA such that I⊂MI\subset M. Then MM is an MZ-space of AA if and only if M/IM/I is an MZ-space of A/IA/I.

Example 1

Let RR be a ring and AA an RR-algebra. Let II be an ideal of AA. Then II is an MZ-space.

Proof. We need to show that r′​(M)⊂s​r​(M)r^{\prime}(M)\subset sr(M). Thus, let a∈r′​(I)a\in r^{\prime}(I) be arbitrary. Then a∈Ia\in I. Since II is an ideal, we have for any b∈Ab\in A that b​an​a∈Iba^{n}a\in I for all n≥0n\geq 0. Therefore a∈s​r​(I)a\in sr(I). △\triangle

3.1 Zhao’s Idempotency Theorem

One of the most important theorems regarding MZ-spaces is Zhao’s Idempotency Theorem:

Theorem 3.1 (Zhao’s Idempotency Theorem [12])

Let kk be a field and AA a kk-algebra. Let MM be a kk-linear subspace of AA such that all elements of r⁡(M)r(M) are algebraic over kk. Then MM is an MZ-space of AA if and only if A​e⊂MAe\subset M for all idempotents ee which belong to MM.

In particular, if MM is an MZ-space of AA and 1∈M1\in M, then M=AM=A.

Corollary 1

Let AA be a kk-algebra and suppose that all elements of r⁡(M)r(M) are algebraic over kk. Then MM is an MZ-space of AA if and only if r⁡(M)r(M) is an ideal of AA.

Not all MZ-spaces are ideals, as the following example shows:

Example 2

The finite field 𝔽4\mathbb{F}_{4} has the following four MZ-spaces:

𝔽4{0}{0,x}{0,x+1}.\displaystyle\mathbb{F}_{4}\qquad\{0\}\qquad\{0,x\}\qquad\{0,x+1\}.

Proof. The sets {0}\{0\}, {0,x}\{0,x\} and {0,x+1}\{0,x+1\} are the only 𝐙{\bf Z}-linear subspaces of 𝔽4\mathbb{F}_{4} that do not contain 11. Since 𝔽4∗\mathbb{F}_{4}^{*} is cyclic, we find that r′​(M)={0}r^{\prime}(M)=\{0\} when MM is a 𝐙{\bf Z}-linear subspace that does not contain 11. It is clear that r′​(M)⊂s​r​(M)r^{\prime}(M)\subset sr(M), thus MM is an MZ-space. △\triangle

3.2 Partial fractions decomposition

We have the partial fractions decomposition of rational maps:

Theorem 3.2

(Partial Fractions Decomposition) Let kk be a field, a1,…,an∈ka_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\in k disinct and α∈k∗\alpha\in k^{*}. Define U(X)=α(X−a1)⋯(X−an)U(X)=\alpha(X-a_{1})\cdots(X-a_{n}) and let V⁡(X)∈k⁡[X]V(X)\in k[X] with degX⁡V⁡(X)<n\deg_{X}V(X)<n be arbitrary. Then

V⁡(X)U⁡(X)=∑i=1nAiX−ai\displaystyle\frac{V(X)}{U(X)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{A_{i}}{X-a_{i}}

with Ai=V⁡(ai)U′​(ai)A_{i}=\frac{V(a_{i})}{U^{\prime}(a_{i})}.

Proof

Note first that U′​(ai)≠0U^{\prime}(a_{i})\neq 0 for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. This is since all aia_{i} are distinct and we know that if both U⁡(ai)=0U(a_{i})=0 and U′​(ai)=0U^{\prime}(a_{i})=0, then aia_{i} is a double root of UU. Since this is not the case, and we know that U⁡(ai)=0U(a_{i})=0, we must have U′​(ai)≠0U^{\prime}(a_{i})\neq 0 for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

Then consider the set 𝒱U⁡(X):={V⁡(X)U⁡(X)∣deg⁡V⁡(X)<n}\mathcal{V}_{U(X)}:=\left\{\frac{V(X)}{U(X)}\mid\deg V(X)<n\right\} as a subset of k⁡(X)k(X), the field of rational functions. Since deg⁡V⁡(X)<n\deg V(X)<n, we see that 𝒱U⁡(X)\mathcal{V}_{U(X)} is spanned by the set {1U⁡(X),XU⁡(X),…,Xn−1U⁡(X)}\left\{\frac{1}{U(X)},\frac{X}{U(X)},\ldots,\frac{X^{n-1}}{U(X)}\right\}. It is clearly a kk-linear subspace of k⁡(X)k(X). Indeed, the elements 1U⁡(X),XU⁡(X),…,Xn−1U⁡(X)\frac{1}{U(X)},\frac{X}{U(X)},\ldots,\frac{X^{n-1}}{U(X)} are kk-linearly independent as well. Hence dimk𝒱U⁡(X)=n\dim_{k}\mathcal{V}_{U(X)}=n.

Now consider the elements 1X−a1,…,1X−an\frac{1}{X-a_{1}},\ldots,\frac{1}{X-a_{n}}. One easily verifies that they belong to 𝒱U⁡(X)\mathcal{V}_{U(X)}. We show that they are linearly independent, and hence form a basis. Therefore, suppose that there exist λ1,…,λn∈k\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}\in k such that

∑i=1nλiX−ai=0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{X-a_{i}}=0.

Then also

λ1+∑i=2nλi​(X−a1)X−ai=0.\displaystyle\lambda_{1}+\sum_{i=2}^{n}\frac{\lambda_{i}(X-a_{1})}{X-a_{i}}=0.

By substituting a1a_{1} for XX, we find λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0.

Then ∑i=2nλiX−ai=0\sum_{i=2}^{n}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{X-a_{i}}=0 and we repeat this procedure. We find that indeed 1X−a1,…,1X−an\frac{1}{X-a_{1}},\ldots,\frac{1}{X-a_{n}} are linearly independent.

Since now these elements constitute a basis for 𝒱U⁡(X)\mathcal{V}_{U(X)}, given any V⁡(X)V(X) with deg⁡V⁡(X)<n\deg V(X)<n, we can write

V⁡(X)U⁡(X)=∑i=1nAiX−ai\displaystyle\frac{V(X)}{U(X)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{A_{i}}{X-a_{i}}

for some A1,…,An∈kA_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\in k. We now determine those AiA_{i}. By multiplying both sides with (X−aj)(X-a_{j}) we get

V⁡(X)U⁡(X)⋅(X−aj)=Aj+∑i≠jAi​(X−aj)X−ai.\displaystyle\frac{V(X)}{U(X)}\cdot(X-a_{j})=A_{j}+\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{A_{i}(X-a_{j})}{X-a_{i}}.

Note that the X−ajX-a_{j} cancels with the X−ajX-a_{j} that occurs in U⁡(X)U(X). So we can substitute aja_{j} for XX and obtain

V⁡(aj)U′​(aj)=Aj,\displaystyle\frac{V(a_{j})}{U^{\prime}(a_{j})}=A_{j},

as required. Note that we used that U′​(aj)=α​∏i≠j(aj−ai)U^{\prime}(a_{j})=\alpha\prod_{i\neq j}(a_{j}-a_{i}). ∎

4 The Theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen

In this section we state the Theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen in one dimension. We shall prove a more general theorem later on, adapting a technique by Monsky. Before we do that, we need to discuss some theorems, all of which are self-contained and needed for our proof. At the end, we shall state the Theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen. The first necessary theorem is the Newton-Puiseux Theorem. (See: [8], [9], [10])

Theorem 4.1 (Newton-Puiseux Theorem [8], [9], [10])

Let kk be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and f⁡(X)=∑i=0nai​(t)​Xi∈k⁡((t))​[X]f(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}(t)X^{i}\in k((t))[X] with n:=degX⁡f⁡(X)≥1n:=\deg_{X}f(X)\geq 1. Then there exists some p≥1p\geq 1 such that f⁡(X)f(X) splits completely in linear factors over k⁡((t1/p))k((t^{1/p})).

Next, we need a special ring for our proof:

Definition 4

Let kk be a field and vv a valuation on kk such that kk is complete with respect to vv. Define k⁡[[X,X−1]]k[[X,X^{-1}]] to be the ring of formal series ∑n=−∞∞cn​Xn\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_{n}X^{n} such that lim|n|→∞cn=0\lim_{|n|\to\infty}c_{n}=0.

Proposition 2

Let k=𝐂⁡((z1/p))k={\bf C}((z^{1/p})) and vv the valuation of kk such that v⁡(z1/p)=1/pv(z^{1/p})=1/p. Then 𝐂​[X,X−1]​[[z]]{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}][[z]] is a subring of k⁡[[X,X−1]]k[[X,X^{-1}]].

Proof

Note that 𝐂⁡((z1/p)){\bf C}((z^{1/p})) is complete with respect to vv, one could write z1/p=tz^{1/p}=t, then k=𝐂⁡((t))k={\bf C}((t)) and v⁡(t)=1/pv(t)=1/p. Hence k⁡[[X,X−1]]k[[X,X^{-1}]] is defined.

Let f⁡(z)=a0​(X)+a1​(X)​z+a2​(X)​z2+…f(z)=a_{0}(X)+a_{1}(X)z+a_{2}(X)z^{2}+\ldots be an arbitrary element of 𝐂​[X,X−1]​[[z]]{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}][[z]] and let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be arbitrary. Write this element f⁡(z)=∑n=−∞∞cn​Xnf(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_{n}X^{n}.

We want to determine NN such that |cn|<ε|c_{n}|<\varepsilon for all |n|≥N|n|\geq N. First, observe that v⁡(zi)=i​v​(z)=i/pv(z^{i})=iv(z)=i/p. So |zi|=2−v⁡(zi)=2−i/p<ε|z^{i}|=2^{-v(z^{i})}=2^{-i/p}<\varepsilon if i>p​log2​(1ε)i>p\log_{2}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}).

Write N⁡(ε):=⌈p​log2⁡(1ε)⌉N(\varepsilon):=\lceil p\log_{2}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})\rceil. Then determine

N:=max0≤i≤N⁡(ε)⁡{deg⁡ai​(X),deg⁡ai​(X−1)}.\displaystyle N:=\max_{0\leq i\leq N(\varepsilon)}\{\deg a_{i}(X),\deg a_{i}(X^{-1})\}.

Then, if |n|>N|n|>N, all ziz^{i} contributing to cnc_{n} come from ai​(X)a_{i}(X) with i>N⁡(ε)i>N(\varepsilon). Since |zi|<ε|z^{i}|<\varepsilon if i>N⁡(ε)i>N(\varepsilon), it follows that |cn|<ε|c_{n}|<\varepsilon. Hence |cn|<ε|c_{n}|<\varepsilon if |n|>N|n|>N.

Hence indeed, f⁡(z)∈k⁡[[X,X−1]]f(z)\in k[[X,X^{-1}]], as required. ∎

The theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen is as follows:

Theorem 4.2 (Duistermaat - Van der Kallen [1])

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be nn commutative variables and let MM be the subspace of the Laurent polynomial algebra 𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn,X1−1,…,Xn−1]{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n},X_{1}^{-1},\ldots,X_{n}^{-1}] consisting of those Laurent polynomials with no constant term:

M={f∈𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn,X1−1,…,Xn−1]∣f0=0}.\displaystyle M=\{f\in{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n},X_{1}^{-1},\ldots,X_{n}^{-1}]\mid f_{0}=0\}.

Then MM is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn,X1−1,…,Xn−1]{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n},X_{1}^{-1},\ldots,X_{n}^{-1}].

We omit the proof, and prove a more general theorem, for dimension n=1n=1, in the next section, see Theorem 5.1.

5 Kernels of linear maps: A generalisation of Duistermaat - Van der Kallen in dimension one

In this section we will discuss a generalisation of Duistermaat - Van der Kallen. Note that

φ:𝐂⁡[X,X−1]→𝐂,f↦f0\displaystyle\varphi\colon{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}]\to{\bf C},f\mapsto f_{0}

is a linear map of 𝐂{\bf C}-vector spaces for which φ⁡(XN)=0\varphi(X^{N})=0 for all |N|≥1|N|\geq 1. The theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen can thus be phrased as: Ker⁡φ\operatorname{Ker}\varphi is an MZ-space.

We now investigate arbitrary 𝐂{\bf C}-linear maps of a form, L:𝐂⁡[X,X−1]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}]\to{\bf C} or L:𝐂⁡[X]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X]\to{\bf C}.

Remark 3
  1. 1.

    If LL is injective, i.e., Ker⁡L=0\operatorname{Ker}L=0, then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space.

  2. 2.

    If L=0L=0, i.e., the trivial linear map, then Ker⁡L=𝐂⁡[X,X−1]\operatorname{Ker}L={\bf C}[X,X^{-1}] (or indeed Ker⁡L=𝐂⁡[X]\operatorname{Ker}L={\bf C}[X]), an MZ-space.

From now on, when we write LL is a linear map, we mean a non-trivial non-injective linear map.

Lemma 1

Let L:𝐂⁡[X]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X]\to{\bf C} be a 𝐂{\bf C}-linear map for which there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 such that L⁡(Xn)=0L(X^{n})=0 for all n∈𝐙≥Nn\in{\bf Z}_{\geq N}. Then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X]{\bf C}[X] if and only if L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.

Proof. ⇒:)\Rightarrow:) Suppose that L⁡(1)=0L(1)=0, then 1∈Ker⁡L1\in\operatorname{Ker}L. Since Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X]{\bf C}[X], we find that Ker⁡L=𝐂⁡[X]\operatorname{Ker}L={\bf C}[X], i.e., L=0L=0, a contradiction. So L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.

⇐:)\Leftarrow:) Note that L⁡(XN)=0L(X^{N})=0. So for any f=∑i=0nai​Xif=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}X^{i} we have

L⁡(f​XN)=L⁡(∑i=0nai​Xi+N)=∑i=0nai​L​(Xi+N)=0,\displaystyle L(fX^{N})=L\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}X^{i+N}\right)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}L(X^{i+N})=0,

hence (XN)⊂Ker⁡L(X^{N})\subset\operatorname{Ker}L. Then by Corollary 1 it suffices to show that Ker⁡L/(XN)\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}) is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}). We will also use Zhao’s Theorem. We therefore need to show that all elements in r⁡(Ker⁡L/(XN))r(\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N})) are algebraic over 𝐂{\bf C} and that 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN)​e⊂Ker⁡L/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N})e\subset\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}) for all idempotents ee in Ker⁡L/(XN)\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}).

Note first that Ker⁡L/(XN)⊂𝐂⁡[X]/(XN)\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N})\subset{\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}), hence any idempotent of Ker⁡L/(XN)\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}) is an idempotent of 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}). We start by determining the idempotents of 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}). Since (X)⊂𝐂⁡[X](X)\subset{\bf C}[X] is a maximal ideal, we find that 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}) is a local ring. A local ring has only idempotents 0,10,1. Since L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0, we see that 00 is the only idempotent in Ker⁡L/(XN)\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}), and we trivially have 0⊂Ker⁡L/(XN)0\subset\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}).

Hence it remains to show that every element in r⁡(Ker⁡L/(XN))r(\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N})) is algebraic over 𝐂{\bf C}. Note that

r⁡(Ker⁡L/(XN))⊂𝐂⁡[X]/(XN),\displaystyle r(\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}))\subset{\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}),

and every element of 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}) is algebraic over 𝐂{\bf C} due to its dimension being finite.

Since we now satisfy the hypotheses of Zhao’s Theorem, we find that Ker⁡L/(XN)\operatorname{Ker}L/(X^{N}) is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X]/(XN){\bf C}[X]/(X^{N}) and hence Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X]{\bf C}[X]. △\triangle

Note that the above lemma can be generalized to an arbitrary field kk, with an identical proof. The following is the generalization of the 11-dimensional version of the theorem of Duistermaat and Van der Kallen.

Theorem 5.1

Let L:𝐂⁡[X,X−1]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}]\to{\bf C} be a 𝐂{\bf C}-linear map for which there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 such that L⁡(Xn)=0L(X^{n})=0 for all n∈𝐙≥Nn\in{\bf Z}_{\geq N} and all n∈𝐙≤−Nn\in{\bf Z}_{\leq-N}. Then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X,X−1]{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}] if and only if L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.

The proof of this theorem relies on the following lemmas and is based on the proof of the 11-dimensional Duistermaat-Van der Kallen theorem by Monsky [6], [7] (Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7).

Lemma 2

Let L:𝐂⁡[X,X−1]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X,X^{-1}]\to{\bf C} be a 𝐂{\bf C}-linear map for which there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 such that L⁡(Xn)=0L(X^{n})=0 for all n∈𝐙≥Nn\in{\bf Z}_{\geq N} and all n∈𝐙≤−Nn\in{\bf Z}_{\leq-N}. If L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0 and f∈r′​(Ker⁡L)f\in r^{\prime}(\operatorname{Ker}L), then f∈𝐂⁡[X]f\in{\bf C}[X] or f∈𝐂⁡[X−1]f\in{\bf C}[X^{-1}].

Proof. Suppose f∉𝐂⁡[X]f\not\in{\bf C}[X] and f∉𝐂⁡[X−1]f\not\in{\bf C}[X^{-1}], i.e. f=α​X−s+…+β​Xrf=\alpha X^{-s}+\ldots+\beta X^{r} with α,β≠0\alpha,\beta\neq 0 and s,r≥1s,r\geq 1. Then consider the power series

W⁡(z)=∑j=0∞L⁡(fj)​zj.\displaystyle W(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}L(f^{j})z^{j}.

We will show that W⁡(z)≠1W(z)\neq 1. That is, L⁡(fm)≠0L(f^{m})\neq 0 for some m≥1m\geq 1. This contradicts f∈r′​(Ker⁡L)f\in r^{\prime}(\operatorname{Ker}L).

6 Encore: Generalizations

In this section we list several generalizations of various results we have seen in this paper. The proofs can be found in [11].

Proposition 3

(Generalization of Lemma 1) Let L:𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\to{\bf C} be a 𝐂{\bf C}-linear map for which there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 such that (X1,…,Xn)l⊂Ker⁡L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})^{l}\subset\operatorname{Ker}L for all l≥Nl\geq N. Then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn]{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] if and only if L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.

We cannot prove

Let L:𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\to{\bf C} be a 𝐂{\bf C}-linear map for which there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 such that L⁡(Xim)=0L(X_{i}^{m})=0 for all m∈𝐙≥Nm\in{\bf Z}_{\geq N} and all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. Then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of 𝐂⁡[X1,…,Xn]{\bf C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] if and only if L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.

For this we have the following counterexample:

Example 3

Take n=2n=2 and N=2N=2 in the following form. Let L:𝐂⁡[X1,X2]→𝐂L\colon{\bf C}[X_{1},X_{2}]\to{\bf C} be the 𝐂{\bf C}-linear map given by

L⁡(X1i​X2j)={1if ​i=1​ or ​i=j=00else\displaystyle L(X_{1}^{i}X_{2}^{j})=\begin{cases}1&\mbox{if }i=1\mbox{ or }i=j=0\\ 0&\mbox{else }\end{cases}

Then we have L⁡(1)=1L(1)=1, and L⁡(Xim)=0L(X_{i}^{m})=0 for all m≥2m\geq 2. It is then clear that X2∈r⁡(Ker⁡L)X_{2}\in r(\operatorname{Ker}L) by construction, but X1​X2m∉Ker⁡LX_{1}X_{2}^{m}\not\in\operatorname{Ker}L for all m≥1m\geq 1. Therefore Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is not an MZ-space.

While it is technically not a generalization, we also have the following lemma, which uses the same method-of-proof:

Proposition 4

Let kk be a field, AA a finite-dimensional kk-algebra and 𝔪\mathfrak{m} a maximal ideal of AA. Let L:A→kL\colon A\to k be a kk-linear map for which there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 such that 𝔪l⊂Ker⁡L\mathfrak{m}^{l}\subset\operatorname{Ker}L for all l≥Nl\geq N. Then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of AA if and only if L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.

In this section we discuss a generalization of Zhao’s Idempotency Theorem (Theorem 3.1), that is in the exercises of [3].

Definition 6

Let RR be a ring, SS a multiplicatively closed subset of RR and AA an RR-algebra. An RR-submodule MM of AA is called SS-saturated if we have a∈Ma\in M for all a∈Aa\in A for which there exists some s∈Ss\in S such that s​a∈Msa\in M, i.e.,

{a∈A∣∃s∈S[sa∈M]}⊂M.\displaystyle\{a\in A\mid\exists s\in S[sa\in M]\}\subset M.
Definition 7

Let RR be a ring, SS a multiplicatively closed subset of RR and AA an RR-algebra. Then e∈Ae\in A is an SS-idempotent if there exists some s∈S∖{0}s\in S\setminus\{0\} such that e2=s​ee^{2}=se.

Theorem 6.1 (Generalized Zhao Theorem [3])

Let RR be a domain, S=R∖{0}S=R\setminus\{0\} and AA an RR-algebra. Let MM be an SS-saturated RR-submodule of AA such that all elements of r⁡(M)r(M) are algebraic over RR. Then MM is an MZ-space of AA if and only if for every SS-idempotent ee of AA which belongs to MM we have that for every a∈Aa\in A there exists an s∈Ss\in S such that s​a​e∈Msae\in M.

Using this Generalized Zhao Theorem, we can prove the following generalization of Lemma 1:

Proposition 5

Let RR be a domain and L:R⁡[Y]→RL\colon R[Y]\to R be a linear map such that there exists an N≥1N\geq 1 for which L⁡(Yn)=0L(Y^{n})=0 for all n≥Nn\geq N. Then Ker⁡L\operatorname{Ker}L is an MZ-space of R⁡[Y]R[Y] if and only if L⁡(1)≠0L(1)\neq 0.
